Object oriented programming • The world consists of objects • Basic idea • Every object in reality has a virtual counterpart • Objects cooperate through data exchange and invocation of services • Perspective • “Who does what?” → Properties and capabilities of objects • Algorithmic perspective: “How is it done?” ©2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 50

Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 51



Definition: object and class
• Three aspects characterize objects
• Identity: properties can change, identity is constant Ensured by name (reference)
• State: set of properties at a point in time Realized by attributes
• Behavior: execution of actions that change the state Realized by methods
• A class is a "blueprint" for similar objects and determines
• Which attributes the objects have
• Which methods the objects have
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 52

import java.util.Date;
class Book {
// Attributes
String author;
String title;
int edition;
//...
// Constructor
Book() {
//... initialize the object
}
// Methods

//...
}

//...
}
}

body
}

Variables • The attributes (data components) of an object are also called instance • Later we will learn about other variables that are defined for • Classes • Methods (locally defined) • Variables must be declared • A constructor must be called (except for so-called basic types) © 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - WO1 Introduction 56

Example: rationale numbers
A rationale number q ∈ Q has the form q = x/y, where x, y ∈ Z
x and y are called numerator and denominator of q
An object of type Rational should contain two int variables numerator and denominator as components (attributes)
Object
numerator
denominator
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 57

Example: rationale numbers
Code
class Rational {
int numerator; // Declaration of an int attribute
int denominator; // Declaration of an int attribute
// constructor Rational() exists automatically
// methods . . .
}
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 58

Declaration and constructor
Rational r declares a variable for objects of the class Rational
The command new Rational(...) creates the object, calls a constructor for this object and returns the new object
Rational r = new Rational(); r.numerator = 3; r.denominator = 4;
numerator 3 denominator 4
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 59

Constructors
• The constructor is a special method that reserves memory in the context of new (and can initialize attributes of the new object)
• Constructors always carry the name of their class
• A default constructor ClassName() in the class ClassName is provided automatically (if no other constructor is defined)
• Constructors can also have arguments
• If you add a custom constructor (with parameters), the default one is not automatically available anymore
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 60

Object references
The value of a Rational variable is a reference
Rational s = r; copies the reference from r to the variable s

Example: points in R2Codeclass Point {double x;double y;// constructor Point() exists automatically// methods . . .}© 2024 Stephan KruscheIntroduction to Programming - W01 Introduction64

Create points / references
• Create points with the keywords new
• Point p = new Point(); // create Point p
• Point q = new Point(); // create Point q
• p, q are names for references to new objects of the class Point
• A point can have multiple identifiers
• Point r = p; // r, p reference the same object
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 65

Functionality of references (1) • Consider two declarations of local variables • Point p; • int n; • Both variables are not (yet) initialized • Initialize • p = new Point(); • n = 5; • new Point() creates an object of type Point (on the heap) and returns a reference to the object • This reference is stored in the reference variable p • n = 5 stores the value 5 directly in the variable n © 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 66 Question: what is their current (default) value?

Functionality of references (2)
Consider two other variable declarations
Point p = new Point();
Point q = p; Store the value of p in the variable q
int n = 5;
int k = n; Store the value of n in the variable k
In case of a reference this is the reference to the respective object
In case of a primitive (basic) type, it is the value itself
p and q refer to one and the same object
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - WO1 Introduction 67

Example: objects as attributes of objects: lines in R² y₂ p₂ y₁ p₁ x₁ x₂ © 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 68

Example: objects as attributes: lines in R²
Code
class Line {
// attributes: end points
Point p1;
Point p2;
// Default constructor Line() no longer exists
// if another constructor is defined.
// Here: constructor explicitly with two arguments!
Line(Point p, Point q) {
p1 = p;
p2 = q;
}
// other methods . . .
}
© 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 69

Example: objects as attributes: lines in R² Code: creation of objects Point p1 = new Point(); p1.x = 2.0; p1.y = 2.7; Point p2 = new Point(); p2.x = 5.8; p2.y = 16.0; Line l = new Line(p1, p2); Improved example with a constructor Point p1 = new Point(2.0, 2.7); Point p2 = new Point(5.8, 16.0); Line l = new Line(p1, p2); class Point { double x; double y; Point(double x, double y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } // methods Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 70

null• The default value for all reference types is null• If a reference variable or a reference attribute have not been initialized, then it has the value null• If a variable has the value null, it does not refer to any object• Example: Point p; // now applies: p == null• Access to p.x and p.y with p == null leads to runtime error!NullPointerException© 2024 Stephan KruscheIntroduction to Programming - W01 Introduction71

Information hiding is an important concept in computer science. Why are endpoints not represented by two coordinate pairs x1, y1 and x2, y2 in class Line? Change of implementation of Point would require a change of implementation of Line (e.g. when changing to polar coordinates). → The implementation of Points is the secret of the class Point alone. This is the only way to limit the effects of changes locally (principle of locality). © 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 72

Intermediate summary • The (virtual) world consists of objects • Objects are instances of classes, classes are blueprints / templates for objects • Objects encapsulate data (attributes) and behavior (methods) • Objects are accessed via references • References are defined by attribute declarations • Attributes can be objects themselves • Objects are created / initialized by new • new always calls a constructor that performs initializations • Two references can point to the same memory area (aliasing) © 2024 Stephan Krusche Introduction to Programming - W01 Introduction 73
